extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and theatre practitioners reading or producing Greek tragedy (especially Euripides)
extracted.subtask_description: Critical commentary and evaluative observations about Euripides' Electra, comparing its style, psychology, moral treatment, and construction with Aeschylus, Sophocles and Homer; useful for assessing productions or literary readings of the play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protest against conventional classicism
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is essentially, and perhaps consciously, a protest against those standards." (the play is judged against conventional classicism and deliberately departs from it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why contemporary classicists (e.g. Schlegel) judged the play harshly; use as an evaluative lens to ask whether the work intentionally subverts classical norms and to what effect. Example criticisms cited: 'A singular monument of poetical, or rather unpoetical perversity;' 'the very worst of all his pieces.' Use these to illustrate how reception varies by critical standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close-knit, powerful, well-constructed play (structural integrity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The play is described as "a close-knit, powerful, well-constructed play."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess structural qualities: unity, tight plotting, dramatic economy. Treat 'well-constructed' as a standard distinct from poetic splendor — a measure of dramatic craft and cohesion rather than lyric grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realism and psychological depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Euripides' Electra is "as realistic as the tragic conventions will allow, intellectual and rebellious. Its psychology reminds one of Browning, or even of Ibsen."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate degree of psychological realism, complexity of motivations, interiority of characters; compare to modern realist/psychological authors. Look for nuanced motives, inner conflict, and 'real people' characterization rather than archetypal figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of legend/history vs heroic atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrasts with Homer and Sophocles: Homer presents the story "simply and grandly, without moral questioning and without intensity" (a heroic atmosphere), while Sophocles aims at an archaic or 'Homeric' style; Euripides interrogates legend and moral assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the play preserves mythic/heroic grandeur or reframes legend as a problem to be examined. Consider whether the treatment foregrounds heroic certainties or moral/psychological ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral interrogation of matricide and divine command
rubrics_metrics.description: Euripides treats the mother-murder as "a sin and a horror" and argues that the god who enjoined it 'did command evil' — the play questions divine authority and the morality of revenge, unlike Aeschylus who frames matricide as a sin that 'must be committed' and expiated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as criterion: does the play present vengeance/matricide as duty, sin, or tragic dilemma? Evaluate how divine commands and religious justification are portrayed (as righteous, ambiguous, or demonic) and whether the drama interrogates moral responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth and complexity of Electra's characterization (central heroine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Electra is the "central figure of the tragedy": "A woman shattered in childhood... a poisoned and a haunted woman, eating her heart in ceaseless broodings of hate and love... who is intolerant of poverty..." She is studied 'profoundly' and compared to other tragic heroines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the heroine's interior life, contradictions (hate and love), social desires (longing for status), and psychological damage. Evaluate whether the production/text renders Electra as a fully realized, conflicted human rather than a symbol or flat avenger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of Orestes (exile, impulsiveness, vulnerability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Orestes is depicted as "an exile, bred in the desperate hopes and wild schemes of exile;... a prince without a kingdom, always dreaming of his wrongs... subject to overpowering impulses and to fits of will-less brooding."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the brother's characterization: his psychological fragility, susceptibility to extremes, and motivation for revenge. Consider whether he appears a sympathetic agent, an instrument of fate/oracle, or a man driven beyond reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of stage-villains; search for 'real people'
rubrics_metrics.description: "A 'sympathetic' hero and heroine are out of the question; and Euripides does not deal in stage villains. He seeks real people."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a standard to judge characterization: look for complexity, moral ambiguity, and humanizing detail rather than simple villainy or idealized heroism. Critique should focus on realism and nuanced motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast between religious/emotional spectacle and intellectual skepticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Aeschylus confronts horror with a "great wave of religious emotion" and sees matricide as sin to be expiated; Euripides "represents intellectually the thought of Aeschylus carried a step further" and treats the god as 'only a demon of old superstition' acting upon men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the play favors religious/cathartic framing (expiation, communal ritual) or intellectual/skeptical inquiry (moral critique, psychological cause). This dimension guides judgments about tone, thematic emphasis, and the play's philosophical stance.
